messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amina is a forty-seven-year-old plumber who grew up in a household where her uncle, who lived with the family for several years when she was a child, would hit her for what he called her “sass.” She remembers the sound of his voice, low and suddenly quiet before he struck her, and the way he would say her name—Amina—as a warning. The physical pain faded, but what stayed was the feeling she was being punished because she was fundamentally bad. She came to believe that the event happened to her because of the sort of person she was, that there was something wrong with her as a person, and that this defect explained why she deserved what she got.

In her daily life as a plumber, Amina often works in people’s basements or crawl spaces, and she sometimes hears a customer call out a name that sounds like hers. When she does, her heart drops. A woman’s voice from another room, a man’s voice on the phone—any voice that carries that same quiet, warning tone—can make her freeze. These triggers immediately feed her old appraisals: she feels defective all over again, as if the sound itself proves she is the kind of person who invites punishment. And because she already believes she is fundamentally wrong, she is hypervigilant for those sounds, listening for them in every job, every conversation, so that she is primed to hear them even when they are not there.

To manage this, Amina has developed strategies that feel protective but have only deepened her isolation. She avoids being around people in authority or uniform—she will not work on commercial buildings where a foreman or inspector might stop by, and she has turned down jobs where a client is a police officer or a school principal. She also avoids anything that reminds her of her uncle: she will not drive past his old neighborhood, she has stopped watching movies with characters named Amina, and she has thrown away old photographs. She dwells on what other people have done to her, replaying her uncle’s cruelty in her mind late at night, and this rumination reinforces her sense that she is a marked person, someone who was chosen for abuse because she was already broken. These strategies make her feel briefly safer, but they also confirm her negative appraisals. She thinks, *If I have to avoid so much, there must really be something wrong with me.* And because she is constantly avoiding, she never gives herself the chance to encounter a neutral or safe voice or name, so her triggers remain potent and her appraisals unchallenged.

Over the months, this cycle has tightened. She has lost two regular plumbing contracts because she refused to work on sites with uniformed security guards. Her husband has grown frustrated with her refusal to attend family gatherings where her uncle’s name might come up. She feels that nothing in her life feels meaningful anymore—she used to take pride in fixing pipes, in being reliable, but now she just feels tired and ashamed. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment last week when she was under a sink and heard a customer’s television playing a show with a character named Amina. She dropped her wrench, crawled out, and said she had to leave. She sat in her truck for an hour, shaking. She is afraid that she is losing her grip on her work and her marriage, and she is most afraid that the therapist will confirm what she already suspects: that there is something fundamentally wrong with her, and that nothing can fix it.
